newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks end off despite soothing economic data.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks end off despite soothing economic data.

text.p: Wall Street stocks ended lower as the U.S. elections neared, see-sawing with bonds after being driven higher early after fresh data reaffirmed moderating economic growth and then easing on profit-taking.

"A lot of traders have stepped to the sidelines to see what the elections will bring. There's the fear of the Democrats carrying both houses of Congress and there might be a nervous reaction fearing a return of an inflationary scenario," said Thom Brown of Rutherford Brown and Catherwood.
The Dow industrials lost seven to about 6022.
For the week, the blue chip index rose 15 points.
Losers outpaced winners 12-11 on very heavy NYSE volume of about 463 million shares.
The S&P 500 index fell two to about 704.
The Nasdaq Composite rose fractionally to about 1222.

The long bond lost 14/32, boosting its yield to 6.68 percent. The yield briefly touched a fresh seven-month low of 6.59 percent after news that October non-farm payrolls rose 210,000, in line with forecasts. Average earnings per hour was unchanged at $11.91. Later came news that the National Association of Purchasing Managers index fell more than expected to 50.2.
The NAPM prices index fell to 47.1 from 51.2 in September.
September U.S. leading indicators rose 0.1 percent and September factory orders rose 2.7 percent.

Tom Carpenter, chief economist at ASB Capital Management Inc, said, "Virtually all the economic data we've seen this week suggests that at the November 13 FOMC meeting, talk will begin on an easing. I don't expect a change that day (on monetary policy) but just talk of."
As for next week's action, Brown, a managing director of Rutherford Brown and Catherwood, said, "The (Tuesday) election is pretty much holding the spotlight until Wednesday morning."

President Bill Clinton's re-election has been largely anticipated, so Wall Street's worry has shifted to the possibility of a Democratic sweep of the Congressional races that may bring more "tax and spending.", analysts said

Brown noted that stocks fell swiftly late Friday "on the sudden sell-off in bond prices. I think we've got a bad case of pre-election nervousness setting in. People will wait and see if there are any surprises before making heavy commitments."
Carpenter said, "It's a day where stocks are keying off bonds, which are down but had a great run the last two weeks."

An afternoon focus for stocks was MCI Communications as rumors swirled that it was in merger talks with British Telecommunications, which has a 20 percent stake in MCI. MCI shares were halted, with the last trade at 30-1/4, up 5-1/8.
Both companies subsequently confirmed there were in talks that would be concluded this weekend.
The news stoked buying in Sprint, up 4-1/2 to 43-3/4, and some Regional Bells with Bell Atlantic, up 1/4 to 60-1/2, NYNEX up 1/2 to 45, PacTel up 1/8 to 34-1/8 and Ameritech, up 1/8 to 54-7/8.
Several IPOs also drew heaby interest.

Ingram Micro, the world's largest distributor of computer hardware, software and networking equipment, rose 2-5/8 to 20-5/8. New Holland NV, a manufacturer of agricultural and heavy machinery, owned by Fiat SpA, was off 3/8 to 21-1/8.
Delta Financial surged 4-7/8 to 21-3/8 and Prime Service, the second-largest U.S. rental equipment company, rose one to 24-1/2, in their first day of trading.
Among other special situations, Inference Corp lost 5-1/4 to seven after the client/server software producer warned that third-quarter results will be well below expectations.
Food Lion class A rose 9/16 to 9-1/8.
The company said it would acquire Kash n' Karry for $26 a share in cash. Kash n' Karry rose 1-1/2 to 25-1/2.
Samsonite Luggage surged 3-3/16 to 36-15/16 after announcing a restructuring and plans to cut 450 positions late Thursday .
The Nasdaq Composite rose 0.27 to 1221.78.
The S&P 500 index fell 1.50 to 703.77.
(Figures official as of 1645 EST/2145 GMT)
-- Wall Street desk 212 859 1721.
